scoreNote: Strong (5): a Claim-appropriate response that takes a clear stand across all three roles, then squarely confronts the most compelling objection and answers it; concrete examples and good control of language.

sentences.text: Whether the setting is a classroom, an office, or a family kitchen, the people in charge face the same daily choice about how to respond when someone does well and when someone falls short.
One popular answer, captured in the claim, is that the best approach in every such role is to praise positive actions and simply ignore negative ones.

Praise is indeed a powerful tool in all three settings, but the claim overreaches, because ignoring negative actions deprives students, employees, and children alike of the correction they need to grow.

sections.role: Body — Where the claim is right

sentences.text: It is true that praise accomplishes a great deal that criticism never can.
A nervous new employee who is thanked for a small success takes on the next task with confidence, just as a child praised for trying hard learns that effort is worth repeating.
Scold a child for every spilled drink and she soon stops trying to pour at all.
Encouragement builds the motivation and trust on which lasting improvement depends, and a manager or parent who notices only failures soon finds people hiding their mistakes rather than fixing them.
Recognition, freely given, makes people want to repeat the very behavior that earned it.
So the claim is right that praise should be the dominant note in teaching of every kind.
However, the instruction to ignore negative actions is where the claim goes badly wrong.

An employee who repeatedly misses deadlines, a student who keeps misunderstanding a concept, a child who treats others unkindly — none of these improves simply because the problem is left unmentioned.
Silence in the face of a fault is not neutrality; it quietly signals approval, the behavior hardens into habit, and everyone nearby draws the lesson that such conduct carries no consequences.
The small unkindness a parent overlooks today can become the cruelty a teacher is forced to confront tomorrow.
A new employee never told that his reports arrive late simply assumes they are fine and keeps filing them late.
In every one of the three roles, refusing to correct is not kindness but neglect dressed up as patience.
The most compelling case for the claim is that correction, clumsily delivered, can crush confidence and breed resentment.
There is real force in this worry, since harsh, public, or relentless criticism does demoralize people and can undo everything praise has built.
But this objection argues against bad correction, not against correction itself, and the remedy is to correct skillfully rather than to fall silent.
Pointing out a fault privately, specifically, and as a problem to be solved together preserves the relationship while still addressing the mistake.
A surgeon who is never told about a sloppy technique will go on endangering patients, however cheerful the operating room.
Handled this way, correction becomes a form of respect, a sign that the teacher, manager, or parent believes the person capable of better.
In conclusion, the claim is half right and half harmful.
In the classroom, the workplace, and the home alike, praise should lead, but ignoring negative actions would leave people to repeat errors that no one was willing to name.
To praise everything indiscriminately is, in the end, to praise nothing at all.
The best teachers, in any role, praise generously and correct kindly, understanding that genuine care sometimes means refusing to look away.
